title: Some More Thoughts on Large Families
author: Foster, Michael
summary: Michael Foster, father of nine (soon ten) children, uses the announcement of an unexpected late pregnancy to share three lessons learned from large-family life. He opens with careful theology: Christians are not obligated to have maximum children (the quiverfull position), but children are a normal part of marriage, and deliberately rejecting all children undermines a central purpose of the marital covenant. He affirms that discernment about family size is real and legitimate, while rejecting abortifacient contraception. The article then offers practical and spiritual formation insights from the experience of having a large family: that the difficulties are genuine (babies in your forties are harder than in your twenties), that the cultural pressure against large families can be acute, and that what a family 'becomes known for' matters more than its size. Foster writes with unusual candor about the mixed emotions of the announcement and positions the piece as an invitation for readers in similar contexts to think carefully about what faithfulness looks like -- not as formula but as ongoing discernment.
points: Foster explicitly rejects both the quiverfull position (Christians obligated to have maximum children) and the assumption that deliberately rejecting children altogether is morally neutral -- positioning his view as a middle ground of discerned fruitfulness.

Having babies in one's forties is genuinely harder than in one's twenties or thirties -- greater physical risk, more complex emotional processing, a cup that 'already overfloweth with responsibility' -- and Foster does not spiritualize these realities away.

What matters is not the number of children but what a family becomes known for: size is not a proxy for faithfulness, and there are good and bad reasons to have or not have children, which are not morally equivalent.

The announcement of a tenth child at ages 42 and 46, after assuming the biological season was closed, is itself a theological illustration of the essay's central point: fruitfulness is not ultimately a human project to manage but a blessing received with gladness and appropriate gravity.

For fathers specifically, the article implicitly makes a formation argument: large families are schools of sacrifice, endurance, and joy that no smaller household configuration fully replicates -- not because they are numerically superior but because they require more of every capacity that matters.
quotes: God designed marriage not only for companionship, but for fruitfulness. Part of filling the world with His glory is filling it with image bearers.

I wrecked my metabolism through poor sleep, bad rhythms, and the kind of constant grind that feels noble in the moment but proves costly over time.
